To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) prostate cancer patients' appraisals of treatment alternatives are based on a combination of the perceived risks and benefits of each alternative; and, 2) oncologists elicit and respond to patients' preferences for treatment by providing them with information on the benefits, risks, and uncertainties of each treatment alternative, and by discussing the treatment options in a non-directive manner.

(1) prostate cancer patients' treatment preferences are not based on the expected health outcomes, but rather on their appraisal of the treatment alternatives and (2) patients' appraisal of the treatment options are influenced by the way their oncologist elicits and responds to patients' preferences and concerns.

(i) patients with advanced prostate cancer appraise the three treatment alternatives (androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), ADT + radiotherapy (RT) and RT) as having similar effectiveness, but different levels of toxicity, (ii) patients with advanced disease prefer ADT + RT over ADT and RT, (iii) patients with localized disease prefer RT over ADT + RT and ADT, and (iv) oncologists do not elicit patients' preferences and do not respond adequately

shared decision making (SDM) is a process that involves patients and clinicians in making a treatment decision.

shared decision-making (SDM) is not a one-size fits-all model.

the patient-physician communication is an important factor in patients' satisfaction with shared decision-making.
